description: Provider bills enormous service volume through only 1-3 HCPCS codes — hallmark of templated phantom claims where the same code is stamped repeatedly
reasoning: Legitimate providers rendering a range of services naturally spread billing across many codes. Extreme concentration (>92nd pct) plus high services-per-patient means nearly every visit generates the same code — the signature of a copy-paste phantom template with no clinical variation.

description: Submitted charges dramatically exceed Medicare's allowed amount — provider sets inflated chargemaster to mask phantom billing by creating apparent 'write-offs'
reasoning: Charge-to-allowed ratios above 95th percentile indicate submitted charges are 3-5x the allowed amount. Legitimate providers rarely inflate charges this aggressively. Combined with moderate-to-high volume, it signals systematic overbilling where phantom claims are camouflaged within a real practice.

description: Very low HCPCS code diversity despite high total payment — provider is generating large revenue from a suspiciously narrow procedure set
reasoning: High payment from very few HCPCS codes (bottom 10% for code count) has no legitimate explanation for general providers. Specialists who happen to bill few codes cluster at low payment; high payment with narrow codes points to phantom claims concentrated on high-reimbursement codes.

description: High dual-eligible concentration with implausibly low risk scores — phantom billing to a vulnerable population whose claims are rarely audited
reasoning: Dual-eligible patients (Medicare+Medicaid) are typically sicker than average, so a provider serving mostly duals should have elevated risk scores. Extremely low risk scores with high dual share indicates the provider is billing duals who are not actually receiving care — classic phantom billing targeting a compliant, hard-to-reach population.

description: Payment per beneficiary is extremely high while services per beneficiary are moderate — suggesting inflated billing tied to paid referrals rather than genuine clinical need
reasoning: Kickback arrangements drive providers to maximize billing on referred patients. Payment-per-bene at 92nd+ pct while services-per-bene is merely elevated (not extreme) suggests billing high-value codes on each visit rather than seeing more patients — consistent with upcoding every referral to generate kickback-worthy revenue.

description: Unusually high fraction of Part B drug HCPCS codes relative to specialty peers — indicates provider is referring patients back to themselves for infusions/injections in exchange for referrals
reasoning: Self-referral kickback schemes often center on infusion suites or injection services with high Part B drug reimbursement. Both the fraction of drug-related payments and drug-related HCPCS codes being simultaneously extreme (vs. specialty peers) has no innocent explanation — legitimate specialists don't systematically concentrate drug administration beyond their peers.

description: High same-day procedure stacking at moderate volume — provider bundles multiple procedures on single visits, consistent with maximizing per-referral revenue
reasoning: Kickback recipients are incentivized to extract maximum revenue per referred patient. Stacking multiple procedures on the same day (above 90th pct for specialty) while charging above-average rates per service suggests deliberate churning of each referral — a pattern rarely seen in legitimate practice.

description: Extreme long-acting opioid claim share — LA opioids (fentanyl patches, methadone, extended-release oxycodone) are the hallmark of chronic pain mills
reasoning: Long-acting opioids require careful titration and are only appropriate for a subset of chronic pain patients. When a provider's LA opioid share exceeds 90th pct for pain specialists AND claims-per-bene is high, patients are receiving repeated LA opioid prescriptions without diversified treatment — the signature of an opioid mill.

description: High opioid claim share combined with high cost per claim — billing expensive branded/extended-release opioids at scale without clinical justification
reasoning: Most legitimate prescribers have diverse drug portfolios; opioids dominating >90th pct of all Part D claims is itself anomalous. Pairing this with high cost-per-claim signals use of expensive branded or high-dose opioids rather than cheap generics — consistent with mills that upsell patients to high-value prescriptions.

description: High opioid share serving a disproportionately under-65 population — younger Medicare patients (SSDI) are the most common opioid mill customers
reasoning: Under-65 Medicare beneficiaries qualify through disability and represent the target demographic for opioid diversion schemes. A pain provider with extreme opioid share AND high under-65 concentration is prescribing to an atypically young, disability-status population — consistent with diversion mills that recruit SSDI patients.

description: Very long average days supply per opioid claim — providers writing 90-day opioid supplies are circumventing visit frequency controls
reasoning: DEA and CMS guidelines discourage long-supply opioid prescriptions except for stable chronic pain. Providers above 90th pct for days-per-claim while also having high opioid share are systematically writing 90-day supplies — maximizing drug quantity per visit, which is the economic model of a mill and facilitates diversion.

description: Near-total saturation of highest-complexity E&M codes — provider never bills low/moderate complexity visits
reasoning: E&M code distribution entropy measures how evenly a provider uses low/moderate/high complexity codes. Legitimate practices see a bell-curve distribution. When high-complexity share exceeds 92nd pct AND entropy is at the bottom 10th pct (meaning almost all codes are high-complexity), the provider is systematically billing every patient at maximum complexity — textbook upcoding with no clinical justification.

description: Payment per service at extreme levels relative to specialty peers — indicates consistent selection of highest-paying code within each service category
reasoning: Within-specialty payment-per-service at 93rd+ pct means this provider consistently bills higher than 93% of peers for the same types of encounters. Pairing with high E&M high-complexity share confirms the mechanism: systematic upcode of every visit to the most expensive code tier.

description: New patient E&M codes billed at high complexity despite high service volume — new patient visits at maximum complexity every time is implausible at scale
reasoning: Providers with few services per beneficiary (low repeat visits) but high E&M complexity billing are turning over many new patients, each billed at maximum complexity. New patient codes (99205, 99215) require exceptional documentation — billing them universally at the highest tier at volume is implausible clinically.

description: Extreme services per beneficiary in specialty contexts where repeat procedures aren't standard — indicates procedure mills ordering unnecessary tests or treatments
reasoning: Legitimate clinical need rarely drives services-per-beneficiary above the 95th percentile for a specialty. At this extreme level, providers are performing procedures on existing patients far beyond peer norms — the billing signature of ordering unnecessary repeat tests, injections, or procedures to maximize revenue per patient in the practice.

description: Very high patient risk scores paired with low-complexity E&M billing — provider is documenting sicker patients to justify high volume but billing conservative codes, suggesting services are not actually rendered
reasoning: Sicker patients (high risk scores) normally generate more complex, better-documented encounters and higher E&M codes. A provider with top-decile risk scores but bottom-15th pct E&M complexity is seeing genuinely ill patients but billing them as straightforward visits — this mismatch suggests either the diagnoses are inflated to justify volume or services are rendered superficially without matching the documented severity.

description: Extreme antibiotic claim share at high prescribing volume — systematically prescribing antibiotics to Medicare patients without evidence of infection
reasoning: Medicare beneficiaries are older and commonly have chronic conditions, but antibiotics should still represent a small share of total prescriptions. Antibiotic claim share at 92nd+ pct combined with high claims-per-bene indicates the provider is reflexively prescribing antibiotics — classic medically unnecessary prescribing that also generates kickbacks from pharmaceutical distributors in some schemes.

description: High telehealth-consistent billing: many services per beneficiary through very few codes — templated telemedicine claim stacking
reasoning: Telehealth fraud schemes generate high claim counts by billing the same visit code repeatedly across large patient panels, often without actual contact. High services-per-bene combined with extreme code concentration (few HCPCS codes used) is the billing fingerprint: the same telehealth visit code applied to many patients, many times, with no clinical variation.

description: High under-65 population concentration with high-complexity E&M saturation — SSDI patients targeted for telehealth fraud schemes
reasoning: Telehealth fraud networks disproportionately recruit disabled under-65 Medicare patients who are homebound and less likely to contest claims. Billing high-complexity E&M codes to this population at scale — without the in-person examination these codes require — is the core mechanism. Both signals above 88th pct simultaneously has no legitimate clinical explanation.

description: Extremely high beneficiary count with low average patient age for specialty — telehealth mills recruit large, younger patient panels that cannot realistically be served
reasoning: A single provider billing Medicare for an extreme number of beneficiaries (top 5%) who are unusually young suggests a telemedicine marketing network that recruits disabled Medicare patients en masse. No single physician can meaningfully serve thousands of patients — this volume is only possible through automated/phantom billing.

description: Home health-adjacent providers with extreme dual-eligible and elderly patient concentration — targeting the highest-dependency patients whose care is hardest to verify
reasoning: HHA fraud relies on patients who cannot easily report whether services were rendered. Dual-eligible patients over 84 are the most vulnerable: cognitively impaired, multi-morbid, and dependent on caregivers. A provider with both signals above 85-90th pct has concentrated their practice in exactly the population used by HHA fraud mills — with no clinical reason to do so unless the referral relationship is financially motivated.

description: Very high risk scores but low medical service fraction — documenting sick patients to justify HHA orders but billing primarily for non-medical (supervisory/administrative) codes
reasoning: Physicians who sign fraudulent HHA certifications tend to document high complexity (to justify homebound status and skilled care orders) but then bill the actual encounter as a brief administrative visit. High risk scores with low medical service fraction exposes this pattern: the patient is being coded as seriously ill but the visit itself is not billed as substantive medical care.

description: High same-day procedure stacking in elderly-heavy practice — billing multiple services on the same day to homebound patients is operationally implausible at scale
reasoning: Stacking multiple procedures on the same visit for very elderly patients is physically challenging and clinically unusual. When both signals exceed 80-90th pct, the provider is regularly billing multiple codes per visit for octogenarian-plus patients — an operational impossibility for a home-visiting practice and a strong signal of claim fabrication.

description: Physicians with extreme drug HCPCS share co-occurring with high drug billing fraction — ordering high-cost DME/supplies under drug codes
reasoning: DME fraud increasingly uses drug HCPCS codes (J-codes) for nebulizers, infusion supplies, and glucose monitors. A provider with both drug HCPCS share and drug payment fraction in the top 10-12% of peers is channeling an anomalous proportion of revenue through drug/supply codes — the billing pattern used by physicians who sign fraudulent DME orders and receive kickbacks.

description: High Part D brand drug share paired with high drug HCPCS share — prescribing branded drugs and ordering brand-name DME supplies as part of a coordinated kickback scheme
reasoning: DME kickback schemes often pair branded drug prescribing with branded equipment orders — both driven by manufacturer kickbacks. A provider simultaneously in the top decile for brand drug share (Part D) and drug/supply HCPCS codes (Part B) is receiving inducements on both sides of the prescribing-and-ordering equation.

description: High dual-eligible concentration with high brand claim share — DME mills target dual-eligible patients because costs are covered by both programs
reasoning: Dual-eligible patients receive both Medicare and Medicaid coverage, making them attractive targets for DME fraud because cost-sharing is minimal and cross-program auditing is weaker. High dual concentration with extreme brand prescribing (vs. peers) suggests the provider is serving a patient base curated for DME fraud recruitment.

description: Extreme services-per-beneficiary in lab/pathology specialty contexts — ordering panels of tests on every patient far beyond clinical need
reasoning: Lab fraud mills order comprehensive panels (urine drug screens, genetic tests, allergy panels) on every patient at every visit. Services-per-bene above 93rd pct means patients average far more services than peers see — no clinical scenario justifies this without a financial motive. High pay-per-bene confirms the lab tests ordered are expensive (e.g., molecular panels, not basic metabolic).

description: Extreme HCPCS code concentration at high volume in a non-procedural specialty — ordering the same test code for every patient repeatedly
reasoning: Lab fraud uses a small set of high-reimbursement test codes (e.g., G0483 comprehensive urine drug screens) applied to every patient. Top-3 concentration above 90th pct combined with high total service count is the specific signature: one or two expensive test codes billed thousands of times, which legitimate ordering physicians never approach.

description: High antibiotic prescribing share combined with extreme services per beneficiary — reflexive culture-and-antibiotic ordering on every patient visit
reasoning: A provider who simultaneously prescribes antibiotics at extreme rates AND orders many services per patient is likely running a culture-and-treat mill: ordering unnecessary microbiology panels to justify antibiotic prescriptions, with the lab billing (to an affiliated lab) and the Rx generating separate revenue streams. The co-occurrence of both signals above 88th pct is rarely innocent.

description: Behavioral health or addiction treatment provider with extreme under-65 population and high opioid prescribing — billing SSDI patients for sober home or treatment services while providing drugs
reasoning: Addiction treatment fraud typically involves billing Medicare for services (counseling, residential) while patients are recruited as opioid diversion conduits. A provider treating predominantly under-65 (disability) patients while simultaneously prescribing opioids at high rates is the operational contradiction at the core of sober home fraud: patients are ostensibly in treatment but receiving opioids.

description: High beneficiary count with very low HCPCS code variety — billing the same addiction treatment code for hundreds of patients without clinical differentiation
reasoning: Addiction treatment centers commit fraud by billing one or two treatment codes (e.g., H0001, H0005) for entire patient populations without individualized care. Extremely high beneficiary count with almost no code variety means every patient receives an identical billing profile — clinically impossible in genuine addiction treatment, which requires individualized assessment and modalities.

description: Simultaneously high long-acting opioid share and antipsychotic-in-elderly share — indicating polypharmacy fraud targeting dual-diagnosis patients
reasoning: Fraudulent addiction/psychiatric practices generate maximum revenue by co-prescribing LA opioids and antipsychotics simultaneously. The combination is clinically contraindicated in most cases (high overdose risk) and represents a pattern seen in body brokering schemes where patients are kept medicated for billing purposes rather than recovery.

description: Provider certifying many very elderly patients with surprisingly low risk scores — documenting terminal prognosis for patients whose coding doesn't support serious illness
reasoning: Hospice eligibility requires a prognosis of 6 months or less, which should correlate with high comorbidity burden and elevated risk scores. A provider enrolling predominantly very elderly patients but with low risk scores is certifying patients whose documented condition severity doesn't support terminal prognosis — the billing signature of hospice fraud where providers enroll patients who are frail but not terminal.

description: Extreme dual-eligible and over-84 concentration — hospice fraud mills preferentially recruit elderly dual-eligible patients whose care is difficult to monitor
reasoning: Hospice fraud networks recruit dual-eligible octogenarian patients because their families are less likely to object to enrollment, costs are covered by both programs, and the patients are too ill to self-report. Both concentrations above 90th pct simultaneously defines the target population of a hospice fraud mill with a precision that legitimate end-of-life practices do not reach.

description: High payment per beneficiary with low E&M complexity — billing for hospice attendance but documenting visits as simple encounters
reasoning: Hospice fraud involves billing for physician attendance at levels that exceed actual visits. High payment-per-bene with low E&M complexity billing means revenue isn't coming from complex documented encounters — it's coming from other codes (e.g., prolonged services, care management codes) billed without supporting documentation of actual clinical time.

description: Very low beneficiary count with extreme code concentration and high payment — someone billing under a stolen NPI uses a handful of fraudulent claims
reasoning: NPI theft uses a legitimate physician's identity to submit a small number of high-value fraudulent claims before detection. The fraud signature is extreme code concentration (the thief picks one or two high-paying codes) combined with high payment per service, at low total volume. The volume floor is intentionally low because NPI theft is often caught early — requiring only a minimum of 11 beneficiaries to eliminate noise.

description: Submitted charges vastly exceed allowed amounts at low volume — suggests a fraudster unfamiliar with actual fee schedules submitting inflated charges under a stolen NPI
reasoning: NPI thieves often do not know the legitimate fee schedule for the specialty they are impersonating. Submitting charges far above the allowed amount (97th pct) at low total beneficiary count (bottom 20th pct) flags providers who are either just starting billing under a stolen identity or are testing the system with inflated phantom claims.

description: Extreme dual-eligible concentration with very low average age — demographic profile inconsistent with the legitimate provider's specialty or region
reasoning: NPI theft often targets beneficiaries in different geographic regions than where the legitimate provider practices. High dual-eligible concentration (low-income urban populations) combined with very young average age (SSDI patients) at low volume suggests a fraudster billing under a stolen NPI in a market the legitimate provider has never served — a demographic mismatch that triggers geographic inconsistency audits.

description: Provider billing only 1-2 HCPCS codes with maximum payment per service — hallmark of a fraudster who selected the highest-paying code to exploit before detection
reasoning: Legitimate providers bill across a range of codes reflecting actual clinical work. A provider in the bottom 5% for code variety while simultaneously in the top 8% for payment per service is almost certainly billing a single high-paying code repeatedly — the simplest form of NPI theft where the criminal picks one lucrative procedure code and submits it under the stolen identity.

description: Very high service volume to an implausibly young and low-acuity population — billing a large number of services to patients whose demographics suggest minimal need
reasoning: Young Medicare patients (SSDI) have lower acuity on average than elderly patients, yet billing high total services to this demographic suggests churning: generating claim volume on patients who require less care. This is the moderate-volume phantom billing pattern — not the most extreme outlier, but a provider who has built a steady phantom-claim factory targeting a recruited SSDI panel.

description: Low E&M distribution entropy with high payment per beneficiary — provider has collapsed all visit types into the highest-complexity tier
reasoning: Entropy near zero means the provider bills a single E&M code for nearly every encounter. Combined with high payment-per-bene, the only codes being billed are the highest-complexity tier. Real practices have diverse patient needs requiring diverse E&M levels — this uniformity is the statistical signature of systematic upcoding.

description: Extreme antipsychotic prescribing to elderly patients — chemical restraint or unnecessary psychiatric medication of nursing-home-adjacent Medicare patients
reasoning: Antipsychotics in the elderly carry a Black Box Warning and CMS has specific nursing home quality measures targeting their misuse. A provider with both extreme antipsychotic share (vs. prescribing peers) and an elderly-skewed population is systematically medicating octogenarians with antipsychotics — either as chemical restraint in a facility setting or as medically unnecessary prescribing driven by kickbacks from long-term care operators.

description: Extreme opioid cost per beneficiary — prescribing very expensive opioid formulations (branded ER, abuse-deterrent) at scale
reasoning: The combination of high opioid share and high cost-per-beneficiary (rather than cost-per-claim) means patients are receiving many expensive opioid prescriptions over time — consistent with long-term opioid mill patients maintained on high-cost branded products. This pattern captures mills that space out prescriptions to avoid per-claim flags while still generating extreme per-patient opioid spend.

description: High payment but low medical service fraction — billing primarily through non-medical codes (care management, chronic care) that are telehealth-accessible and less auditable
reasoning: Telehealth fraud increasingly exploits chronic care management (CCM) and remote patient monitoring codes that do not require synchronous visits. A provider generating high per-bene revenue but with low medical service fraction is extracting value through care management codes billed without clinical contact — a billing pattern that requires no equipment, no patient presence, and is very difficult to disprove.

description: High services per beneficiary concentrated in very elderly patients — billing for repeated home visits that were not made
reasoning: HHA fraud often involves physicians who sign off on care plans and then bill for supervision visits that were never made. A physician with high services-per-bene concentrated in the oldest-old population is claiming to have made many clinical contacts with extremely frail patients — physically implausible at scale and a signature of fraudulent home visit billing.

description: High same-day procedure stacking combined with extreme drug HCPCS share — billing multiple drug/DME codes on the same visit
reasoning: DME fraud schemes that also involve infusion suites or supply dispensing stack multiple drug/supply codes on the same visit. High same-day stacking plus extreme drug HCPCS share means the provider routinely bills several drug-related codes per encounter — consistent with a medical office that has co-located a DME supplier and bills every dispensed item as a separate service on the same date.

description: High brand drug share in a practice with very elderly patients — prescribing expensive branded medications to ostensibly terminal patients who should be on comfort-focused generic regimens
reasoning: Legitimate hospice-adjacent prescribing emphasizes comfort care with inexpensive generics (morphine, lorazepam). A provider certifying very elderly patients for hospice while simultaneously prescribing expensive branded drugs is contradicting the clinical logic of palliative care — indicating patients are neither truly terminal nor receiving hospice-appropriate treatment, while maximizing both Part B hospice certification billing and Part D brand drug revenue.

description: Extreme payment per service with narrow code concentration — ordering only the most expensive lab panels (molecular, genetic) repeatedly
reasoning: Lab fraud maximizes revenue by selecting the highest-reimbursing test codes (genetic panels, comprehensive drug screening, molecular pathology). Payment-per-service above 92nd pct means the tests being ordered are consistently among the most expensive available. Combined with high code concentration, the provider is ordering the same expensive test panel for nearly every patient — no clinical rationale justifies this without financial motivation.

description: High cost per beneficiary with low procedure variety — extracting maximum revenue per patient through a narrow set of high-value services, consistent with a referral arrangement requiring specific procedures
reasoning: Kickback arrangements often specify which procedures the receiving provider must perform to trigger the kickback payment. This creates a profile where pay-per-bene is very high (driven by expensive mandated procedures) but code variety is low (the provider limits themselves to the agreed procedures). High revenue extraction through a narrow, high-value procedure set is a structural signal of a kickback contract.
